findings.claim: On a hang restart, the new guard `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for spawn-context processes, so `kill()` never runs. A replacement then starts on the same shards while the old process keeps running. The replacement takes over the `process_healthy_since` slot, so nothing monitors the old process. Two flushers can then read the same segments and produce duplicates, and up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS (10) orphaned processes per index can pile up, each holding Redis and Kafka connections. Before the patch, `kill()` was called unconditionally.
findings.evidence: Processes are built by `multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process`, which is SpawnProcess with MRO (SpawnProcess, BaseProcess, object). Three seats ran the one-liner `python3 -I -c "import multiprocessing as m; p=m.get_context('spawn').Process(target=print); print(isinstance(p, m.Process))"`: it prints False (mattpocock got AssertionError from the assert form). No seat wrote a full flusher test. Severity was normalised to Important: superpowers rated it Critical, the other three Important.
findings.reason: Accepted. All four seats agree, and the root cause reproduces with a stdlib command on the pinned interpreter. Red test to write before fixing: make `healthy_since` look stale, call `submit()` so `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts the process, then assert the old process is no longer alive. That test needs the Sentry test environment. Smallest fix: check `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`.

verifier.reason: At flusher.py:254 the patch kills only when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, but processes come from `get_context('spawn').Process` (flusher.py:53, 105). In CPython that class is SpawnProcess, which subclasses BaseProcess and not the default-context `multiprocessing.Process`, so a hung process is never killed. flusher.py:259 then starts a replacement on the same shards and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]`, so the old process is no longer tracked and `join` never terminates it (flusher.py:346); the old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally.

findings.claim: In `join`, `terminate()` sits behind the same wrong `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check, so it never runs for SpawnProcess. On shutdown or rebalance, flusher processes are never terminated. The check existed before the patch, but the patch carries it into the new per-process loop.
findings.evidence: Same MRO evidence and one-liner as the kill guard. mattpocock S1 ('Also :346'), the open-code-review #2 caveat, ponytail's out-of-seat note and superpowers #1 'Related' all identify it and all say it predates the patch.
findings.reason: Accepted. It predates the patch but sits on lines the patch rewrites, and it shares the root cause and the one-line fix of the kill-guard finding. Red test: start the flusher, call `join(timeout)`, and assert every process is no longer alive. That fails on the pinned code.

verifier.reason: At flusher.py:346, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for the `SpawnProcess` objects created by `self.mp_context.Process` (flusher.py:105). In CPython, `multiprocessing.Process` is `context.Process`, and `SpawnProcess` inherits only from `process.BaseProcess`, so `terminate()` at :347 is never called. The same check existed before the patch (pre-patch `isinstance(self.process, multiprocessing.Process)`), and the patch moved it into the per-process loop. In practice a flusher usually exits on its own once the `stopped` flag is set, and it is a daemon process, so only one that is still running at the deadline is left alive.

findings.claim: In `join`, once the deadline has passed, the `remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the loop before `terminate()` runs for the current process and for every later one. The base code always reached its terminate step. The guard bug at :346 currently hides this, and it becomes a live gap as soon as that guard is fixed.
findings.evidence: Reasoned from code by all three seats (lines 336-347); no command was run. Severity was normalised to Important: open-code-review rated it Important, superpowers Minor, and ponytail nice-to-have.

verifier.reason: In flusher.py:337-347, once the deadline passes, the `break` at :341 leaves the loop before the `terminate()` at :347 runs for the current process and every later one; the base code always reached its single terminate step. The `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard at :346 is never true for a spawn-context `SpawnProcess`, so terminate is a no-op today and the gap only shows once that guard is fixed.

findings.claim: Each process gets its own `SpansBuffer(shards)` holding only its subset of shards, so `ceil(max_flush_segments / len(assigned_shards))` is now computed per process. `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` therefore silently becomes a per-process budget, so the total flush per cycle scales with the process count. The `any_shard_at_limit` backpressure threshold rises too, which delays backpressure.
findings.evidence: Reasoned and not run. Cited at src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:382-384,410 and flusher.py:64-66. The option is documented as per cycle at src/sentry/options/defaults.py:2716. The CLI default of 1 is unaffected, but `max_processes=None` and any flag value above 1 are affected. mattpocock listed this under 'Not checked (outside this seat)'.
findings.reason: Accepted and unverified. Red test: with 2 flusher processes and max-flush-segments=K, seed more than K segments across all shards and assert that at most K are flushed per cycle. Smallest fix: divide the per-process budget by the process count.

verifier.reason: The patch gives each process a `SpansBuffer(shards)` holding only its shard subset (flusher.py:152). That buffer's `flush_segments` divides the option by `len(self.assigned_shards)` (buffer.py:382-384), so each process can fetch up to the full `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments`, which defaults.py:2716 documents as a per-cycle limit, and the total grows with the process count. The `any_shard_at_limit` threshold at buffer.py:411 rises the same way, so `backpressure_since` (flusher.py:172) gets set later.

findings.claim: The parent keeps one `SpansBuffer` per child, and every `submit()` loops over all of them. That means N `record_stored_segments` pipelines and N cluster-wide `get_memory_info` INFO calls against the same Redis cluster, where one call used to do. The memory ratio is unchanged because the duplicates cancel out. The extra calls add I/O on the consumer main thread and return nothing new.
findings.evidence: Reasoned. Lines 269-270 and 299-301. All buffers use `get_redis_client()` on SENTRY_SPAN_BUFFER_CLUSTER (buffer.py:117).
findings.reason: Accepted. Keep a single `self.buffer` covering all shards in the parent, and drop the `self.buffers` loops and the ServiceMemory import.

verifier.reason: submit() loops over self.buffers at flusher.py:269-270 and 299-301. Each SpansBuffer's get_memory_info() is iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client) on the same SENTRY_SPAN_BUFFER_CLUSTER (buffer.py:117-118, 375-376), so the cluster-wide INFO runs N times with duplicate results and the used/available ratio does not change. record_stored_segments (buffer.py:357-364) is split across disjoint shard subsets rather than duplicated, but it still makes N pipeline round trips where one used to do.
